posts.text:
At its peak, the British Empire ruled about a quarter of the world's land surface and roughly 458 million people.

This map plots every year a piece of it broke away — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ It started early: the United States declared independence in 1776, nearly a century and a half before the empire even reached its largest size. The 13 colonies were gone before Britain had finished building the rest.

2/ The "white dominions" left quietly, by law rather than war. The Statute of Westminster in 1931 gave Canada, Australia, South Africa and the Irish Free State full legislative independence — no revolution, just an act of Parliament in London.
3/ Ireland's path was different: the Irish Free State was created in 1922 after a guerrilla war and a treaty partitioning the island — a rupture that still shapes politics in Northern Ireland today.

4/ Then came the wave. India and Pakistan split from Britain and each other in August 1947, ending nearly 90 years of direct Crown rule over the subcontinent and displacing an estimated 10-15 million people in the partition.

5/ 1960 alone saw 17 African nations gain independence, including Nigeria — historians call it the "Year of Africa." Within a decade of that, Britain had handed over Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi and more.
6/ The retreat kept going into the 1980s: Zimbabwe in 1980, Belize in 1981, Brunei in 1984, Hong Kong handed to China in 1997. From a quarter of the globe to 14 overseas territories today.

7/ Same empire, one map, two centuries of countries walking out the door.
